evt-hallstatt-origins: A richly worked Hallstatt-era gold neck-ring from Uttendorf, Austria — the kind of treasure these Iron Age chieftains were rich enough to take into the grave
evt-hallstatt-salt-mines: A Bronze Age timber staircase deep in the Hallstatt salt mine, built around 1344 BCE — the salty air preserved it intact for over three thousand years
evt-hallstatt-dagger-type: Hallstatt-type iron swords from Wels, Austria — long blades made for cutting down from horseback, the left one keeping its ornate decorated pommel
evt-celtic-wine-trade: A bronze cross-handled wine bowl from Hallstatt — the elaborate drinking gear that turned imported Mediterranean wine into the centerpiece of a chieftain's feast
evt-heuneburg: The reconstructed Heuneburg on the upper Danube, its buildings backed by the white mudbrick wall its rulers copied straight from the Greek world around 600 BCE
evt-hallstatt-elite-burials: A cutaway model of a Hallstatt chieftain's grave — a wooden chamber packed with goods, sealed under a huge earthen mound ringed with stone
evt-hochdorf-burial: The reconstructed Hochdorf chieftain's grave near Stuttgart — the dead man laid out on a bronze couch beside a four-wheeled wagon loaded with bronze dishes for the afterlife
evt-vix-burial: The Vix krater, over five feet tall and the largest bronze vessel to survive from antiquity — Greek-made, hauled over the Alps, and buried with a Celtic woman around 500 BCE
evt-celtic-expansion-iberia: A Celtiberian antenna-hilted iron sword — the short, double-edged blade so effective that Rome copied it wholesale as the gladius hispaniensis
evt-golasecca-culture: A decorated bronze situla from a Golasecca grave — the kind of fine metalwork these Alpine middlemen traded between the Mediterranean and the Celtic north
evt-lepontic-inscriptions: The Prestino stone near Como, carved with a line of Lepontic — the oldest surviving Celtic writing, in an alphabet borrowed from the Etruscans
evt-amber-trade: The European Amber Road stretched from the Baltic coast deep into the Mediterranean world, funneling the prized golden resin southward to Mycenaean workshops hungry for exotic prestige materials.
evt-pj-odai-yamamoto: The Odai Yamamoto site in Aomori, where some of the world's oldest pottery was unearthed.
evt-norse-longhouse: Reconstructed Viking chieftain's longhouse at the Lofotr Viking Museum, Vestvågøy, Norway
evt-eridu-temple: Ruins of the ancient Sumerian ziggurat at Eridu, southern Iraq, with stamped bricks from King Ur-Nammu's construction
evt-inanna-worship: The goddess Inanna (Ishtar) depicted on an Akkadian cylinder seal, shown with wings and weapons as the goddess of love and war
evt-wheel-invention: Detail of the Standard of Ur (c. 2600 BCE) showing Sumerian war carts on solid wooden wheels — the earliest depictions of the wheel in use.
evt-cylinder-seal: Cylinder seal and its clay impression showing the king-priest feeding the sacred herd, Uruk period, c. 3200 BCE
evt-cuneiform-invention: A proto-cuneiform tablet from the Oriental Institute Museum, roughly 3100 BCE — an early step from pictographic tokens to wedge-shaped writing.
evt-beer-brewing: The Alulu Beer Receipt (c. 2050 BCE), a Sumerian cuneiform tablet recording a delivery of the finest beer — among the oldest written beer records.
evt-silk-road-precursor: Raw lapis lazuli stone with golden pyrite inclusions, sourced from Afghanistan
evt-elamite-rivalry: Map showing the extent of ancient Elam in relation to Mesopotamia
evt-gilgamesh-person: The Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, a cuneiform fragment of the Epic of Gilgamesh — one of the world's oldest surviving works of literature.
evt-royal-tombs-ur: Black-and-white photograph of the Royal Cemetery of Ur excavations
evt-early-dynastic-wars: The Stele of the Vultures in the Louvre Museum, commemorating a Sumerian military victory
evt-sumerian-trade-networks: Map of the ancient Near East in the 3rd millennium BCE, showing Sumerian maritime trade routes and partner cities
evt-eannatum: Fragment of the Stele of the Vultures showing King Eannatum of Lagash leading troops, Louvre Museum
evt-shekel-weight: Electrum stater coin from Carthage, c. 310–290 BCE, showing the head of Tanit
evt-sumerian-astronomy: The MUL.APIN astronomical tablet at the British Museum — a compilation of star lists, calendar rules, and planetary observations going back to Sumerian times.
evt-lugalzagesi: Akkadian victory stele from the era of Lugal-zage-si, showing a prisoner exiting a cage, c. 2300 BCE, Louvre Museum
evt-sargon-akkad: Bronze head believed to represent an Akkadian king, possibly Sargon or Naram-Sin, Iraq Museum, Baghdad
evt-enheduanna: Calcite disk depicting Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad, history's first known author
evt-naram-sin: Victory Stele of Naram-Sin showing the Akkadian king ascending a mountain over fallen enemies, Louvre Museum
evt-gudea-lagash: Diorite statue of Gudea of Lagash, dedicated to the god Ningishzida, c. 2120 BCE
evt-ur-nammu: Stone carving depicting King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur
evt-code-ur-nammu: Clay tablet fragment bearing the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest surviving law code, Istanbul Archaeological Museum
evt-ziggurat-ur: Remains of the Great Ziggurat of Ur in southern Iraq, originally built c. 2100 BCE
evt-epic-gilgamesh-written: The Flood Tablet (Tablet 11 of the Epic of Gilgamesh), Neo-Assyrian clay tablet from the Library of Ashurbanipal, British Museum
evt-sumerian-king-list: The Weld-Blundell Prism, a four-sided clay prism inscribed with the Sumerian King List
evt-shulgi: Line drawing of a cylinder seal impression attributed to King Shulgi of Ur
evt-mari-kingdom: Ruins of a ziggurat near the royal palace at Mari, Syria
evt-babylonian-mathematics: Clay tablet YBC 7289 from the Yale Babylonian Collection showing a square with diagonal and sexagesimal calculations
evt-plimpton-322: Plimpton 322, a Babylonian clay tablet listing Pythagorean triples, c. 1800 BCE
evt-hammurabi: Votive monument dedicated to Hammurabi, king of Babylon, British Museum
evt-code-hammurabi: Upper portion of the Code of Hammurabi stele showing the king receiving authority from the god Shamash, Louvre Museum
evt-babylon-marduk: The head of a mušḫuššu, Marduk's serpent-dragon, from Babylon — the symbol of the god who rose to supremacy over the Mesopotamian pantheon.
evt-atra-hasis: A Met Museum cuneiform tablet of the Atra-Hasis, the Babylonian flood myth where the gods send a deluge to thin an overpopulated world.
evt-hittite-sack-babylon: "The Fall of Babylon" — mezzotint by John Martin, 1831, depicting Cyrus the Great defeating the Chaldean army
evt-mitanni-kingdom: Map of the Mitanni kingdom at its greatest extent, showing major cities and archaeological sites
evt-amarna-letters: Clay Amarna letters on display at the British Museum — the diplomatic mail that links the Hittite court into the Late Bronze Age great-power club.
evt-tukulti-ninurta: Stone base with cuneiform inscription showing Tukulti-Ninurta I standing and kneeling before a divine symbol, 13th century BCE
evt-assyrian-conquest-babylon: The Statue of Marduk depicted on a 9th-century BCE cylinder seal — Assyrian conquerors carried this sacred statue from Babylon as a trophy of war
evt-nebuchadnezzar-i: Kudurru (boundary stone) from the reign of Nebuchadnezzar I, recording a land grant and tax exemption, 12th century BCE
evt-tiglath-pileser-i: Stone relief depicting Tiglath-Pileser I, king of Assyria
evt-enuma-elish: The Ashmolean's Enuma Elish tablet (AN1926.373) — the Babylonian creation epic that elevated Marduk to king of the gods.
evt-mul-apin: The MUL.APIN tablet — clay tablet with two columns of astronomical text listing star catalogues, British Museum
evt-new-year-festival: Modern Assyrian community celebrating the Akitu (New Year) festival, 2019
evt-ashurnasirpal-ii: Stone relief showing King Ashurnasirpal II meeting a high official during a review of soldiers and prisoners
evt-nimrud: Pair of lamassu (winged human-headed bulls) guarding the entrance to Ashurnasirpal's palace at Nimrud
evt-shalmaneser-iii: Stone relief detail depicting King Shalmaneser III of Assyria
evt-battle-qarqar: The Kurkh Stela of Shalmaneser III, recording the Battle of Qarqar in 853 BCE
evt-babylonian-eclipse: Babylonian clay tablet recording astronomical observations, British Museum
evt-tiglath-pileser-iii: Gypsum wall panel relief of King Tiglath-Pileser III wearing royal robes with a full beard and ceremonial mace
evt-tiglath-pileser-conquests: Map showing Assyrian deportation routes — Tiglath-Pileser III systematized mass population transfers as imperial policy
evt-fall-of-israel: Panel from the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III showing Israelite delegates bearing tribute to the Assyrian king, British Museum
evt-sennacherib: Cast of a rock relief of King Sennacherib from the mountain of Cudi Dağı, near Cizre, Turkey
evt-sennacherib-jerusalem: Remnants of the Broad Wall in Jerusalem, built by King Hezekiah in preparation for Sennacherib's siege
evt-babylonian-zodiac: 19th-century engraving of an Assyrian astronomical scene related to celestial observation
evt-nineveh-capital: The reconstructed Mashki Gate at the ancient site of Nineveh, Iraq
evt-esarhaddon: Basalt victory stele of King Esarhaddon holding ropes attached to conquered rulers, Pergamon Museum, Berlin
evt-assyrian-conquest-egypt: Map of the Neo-Assyrian Empire at its greatest territorial extent, 824–671 BCE
evt-ashurbanipal: Stone relief of King Ashurbanipal hunting a lion from horseback, British Museum
evt-library-nineveh: Cuneiform tablets from the Library of Ashurbanipal on display at the British Museum
evt-destruction-elam: Assyrian relief depicting the destruction of the Elamite city of Hamanu, c. 645–635 BCE
evt-battle-carchemish: Illustration of the Battle of Carchemish from Hutchinson's History of the Nations, 1915
evt-nebuchadnezzar-ii: Artist's reconstruction of the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II
evt-nebuchadnezzar-ii-person: Artist's reconstruction of the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon during the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II
evt-hanging-gardens: 19th-century artist's imagining of the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, inspired by early archaeological excavations
evt-chaldean-dynasty: Map of Babylonia during the Chaldean period, showing the centers of astronomical observation and major cities
evt-etemenanki: Architectural reconstruction drawing of the Etemenanki ziggurat in Babylon
evt-mesopotamia-destruction-jerusalem: 19th-century Bible illustration depicting the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylonian forces
evt-ishtar-gate: Reconstructed Ishtar Gate of Babylon, covered in blue-glazed bricks with relief figures of bulls and dragons, Pergamon Museum, Berlin
evt-nabonidus: Detail of a stele showing King Nabonidus in traditional Babylonian royal dress, holding symbols of authority
evt-fall-babylon-persia: "The Fall of Babylon" — mezzotint by John Martin, 1831, depicting the Persian conquest
evt-mehrgarh-settlement: The mud-brick ruins of Mehrgarh, the farming village at the foot of the hills that was already growing wheat and herding cattle thousands of years before the cities.
evt-ravi-phase-harappa: A relief map of the Indus region pinpointing Harappa on the Ravi River, where the city's earliest village phase began.
evt-kot-diji-founded: The massive walls at Kot Diji, the fortified pre-urban town that gave its name to a whole early Indus culture-phase.
evt-kalibangan-plowed-field: The eroded mound of Kalibangan, the site that preserved the world's oldest known plowed field beneath its early levels.
evt-early-indus-script: A close-up of an early seal impression, a short row of Indus signs that count among the first writing-like marks in the valley.
evt-kot-diji-burned: The Kot Diji citadel looming over the modern town, marking the site where a burned destruction layer cuts across the early settlement.
evt-mature-harappan-begins: The full reach of the Mature Harappan phase, when scattered towns suddenly snapped into one uniform civilization of planned cities.
evt-mohenjo-daro-built: The excavated brick ruins of Mohenjo-daro, with the later Buddhist stupa mound rising over the city the Harappans laid out from scratch.
evt-dholavira-built: The stone walls of Dholavira spreading across a Gujarat plateau, a Harappan city built of dressed stone rather than mud brick.
evt-rakhigarhi: The low, scrub-covered mounds of Rakhigarhi, the sprawling Harappan site on the Indian plains that may rival Mohenjo-daro in size.
evt-urban-planning: The grid of Mohenjo-daro laid bare, straight streets and right-angled blocks showing a city planned on paper before a brick was laid.
evt-harappa-city: An artist's reconstruction of a Harappa street at its peak, mud-brick houses crowding a planned lane lined with covered drains.
evt-drainage-system: Brick-lined drainage channels at Lothal — the Indus cities ran covered street drains that wouldn't be matched for thousands of years.
evt-standardized-weights: Harappan chert cube weights, neatly graduated in size — the same standardized system turns up at city after city across the whole civilization.
evt-indus-script-seals: Six Indus seals and their clay impressions, each topped by a line of the still-undeciphered script above a carefully carved animal.
evt-granaries-harappa: The brick foundations on Mound F at Harappa, long read as the city's great granary or warehouse complex.
evt-bead-making: Etched carnelian and agate beads from Chanhu-daro — the kind of long, hard-stone beads Indus workshops drilled and traded as far as Mesopotamia.
evt-dancing-girl: The bronze Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro, hand on hip and bangles up one arm, cast 4,500 years ago by lost-wax method.
evt-pashupati-seal: The Pashupati seal, a horned figure sitting cross-legged amid animals, often read as an early hint of later Indian religious imagery.
evt-mother-goddess: A terracotta female figurine, hand-modeled with an elaborate headdress and jewelry — the kind of "mother goddess" figure found by the hundreds in Indus homes.
evt-cotton-cultivation: Tree cotton (Gossypium arboreum), the very species the Harappans were the first in the world to domesticate and spin into cloth.
evt-urban-wells: Mohenjo-daro's brick-lined neighborhoods, where nearly every block had its own deep public well sunk into the streets.
evt-lothal-founded: Brick drains and platforms at Lothal, the Gujarat port town with its own dockyard linking the Harappans to the sea.
evt-dholavira-signboard: A reconstruction drawing of the ten giant signs mounted over Dholavira's north gate — possibly the world's oldest signboard, though nobody can read it.
evt-dholavira-reservoirs: One of Dholavira's huge rock-cut reservoirs, part of the elaborate stepped water system that let the city survive in near-desert.
evt-unicorn-seal: The famous one-horned "unicorn" bull — the single most common animal on Indus seals — shown here on a seal and its blown-up cast.
evt-administrative-seals: A steatite stamp seal carved with Indus script (left) and the clay impression it leaves (right) — the paperwork of a trading economy we still can't read.
evt-burial-practices: A Harappan burial laid out full-length with grave goods — the Indus dead were sent off with pottery and ornaments, not monuments.
evt-fortification-walls: The massive mud-brick walls of Mohenjo-daro — less about fending off armies than holding back floods and marking the raised citadel.
evt-ruler-measurement: Brick drainage channel at Lothal — the standardized brick sizes reflect the Indus decimal measurement system
evt-animal-veneration: An elephant carved on a Harappan seal, shown with its raised clay impression — one of many animals the Indus people singled out on their seals.
evt-indus-metallurgy: The Daimabad copper chariot — a driver behind a team of oxen, cast in metal — showing just how far Indus bronze and copper working had come.
evt-toy-carts: Little terracotta Harappan figures including a model bullock cart, the kind of toy that doubles as evidence the Indus people used wheeled carts.
evt-climate-shift: A world map of the 4.2-kiloyear climate event, the global drought pulse that helped tip the Indus cities into decline.
evt-surkotada: A site map of the Indus world with Surkotada marked down in Gujarat, the small fortified town where contested horse bones turned up.
evt-mohenjo-daro-massacre: Human bones excavated at Mohenjo-daro, the scattered 'massacre' skeletons once read as invasion victims but now seen as ordinary late burials.
evt-cemetery-h: Painted burial urns of the Cemetery H culture, the post-urban people who reused Harappa's ground with a new pottery style.
evt-pirak-settlement: A weathered mud-brick graveyard near the Pirak region, the bridge-culture site where horse, camel and rice show the Harappan world giving way to what came next.
evt-vedic-period-begins: A map of the early Vedic world that took shape across the northwest just as the Indus cities were emptying out.
evt-great-bath: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro — a watertight sunken pool of fitted brick, with steps leading down at either end, built more than 4,000 years ago.
evt-priest-king: The Prince of the Lilies (Priest-King) relief fresco from Knossos, a striding figure crowned with lilies and feathers.
evt-uruk-city: The excavated mud-brick remains of Uruk at modern Warka in southern Iraq, the first settlement to cross every threshold that defines a city.
evt-irrigation-systems: A lake below Girnar near the site of the Maurya-built Sudarshana reservoir, a feat of state irrigation.
evt-white-temple-uruk: The remains of the White Temple platform at Uruk — forerunner to the massive stepped ziggurats that would define Mesopotamian sacred architecture.
evt-sexagesimal-system: Plimpton 322, a Babylonian mathematical tablet listing Pythagorean triples in base-60 — evidence that Sumerian math was far more sophisticated than a counting tool.
evt-temple-economy: A Sumerian administrative tablet from Istanbul — the kind of daily ration record that ran the temple economy.
evt-flood-narrative: The Sumerian Flood Story tablet (CBS 10673) at the Penn Museum — a millennium older than the biblical Genesis flood account.
evt-gutian-invasion: A 19th-century illustration of the Gutians sacking a Mesopotamian city — the mountain people whose raids ended the Akkadian Empire.
evt-fall-of-ur: The Lamentation over the Destruction of Ur (Louvre AO 6446), a Sumerian poem mourning the fall of Ur III to the Elamites.
evt-isin-larsa: An Isin-Larsa period cylinder seal — the era when rival Sumerian kings at Isin and Larsa divided the south before Hammurabi's Babylon swallowed them both.
evt-old-assyrian-trade: The excavated Assyrian merchant colony (karum) at Kanesh in central Anatolia — thousands of cuneiform business letters documenting the trade network were found here.
evt-descent-of-inanna: The British Museum's tablet of Ishtar's Descent to the Underworld (K.162) — the Akkadian version of Inanna's katabasis through seven gates.
evt-kassite-dynasty: A kudurru — a Kassite-period boundary stone carved with divine symbols, the signature legal document of the dynasty that ruled Babylon for over 400 years.
evt-aramean-migrations: Sculptural orthostats from the Aramaean palace at Tell Halaf in Syria (c. 9th century BCE) — the wave of migrants whose Aramaic would eventually replace Akkadian across the region.
evt-battle-halule: An Assyrian relief of King Sennacherib, who commanded the Assyrian army at Halule in 691 BCE — both sides claimed victory.
evt-nabopolassar: A foundation cylinder of Nabopolassar from Babylon — the Chaldean king who founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire by breaking Assyria's grip on the south.
evt-cre-birmingham-campaign: Birmingham, May 1963: young demonstrators huddle in a doorway as firefighters turn high-pressure hoses on them during the SCLC Birmingham campaign (Project C).
evt-xiongnu-battle-ikh-bayan: The Altai mountain region, the rugged borderland where Han and allied forces shattered the Northern Xiongnu at Ikh Bayan and ended their hold on the Mongolian steppe.
evt-genoese-caffa: The Genoese fortress towers at Caffa (modern Feodosia, Crimea), the Black Sea colony the Mongols besieged in 1346.
evt-knossos-palace: The North Entrance of Knossos, its restored red columns and bull fresco marking the largest of the Minoan palaces.
evt-baekje-founding: Baekje at its 4th-century reach along the peninsula's southwest.
evt-mi-shastri-pm: Lal Bahadur Shastri, who became prime minister of India in 1964 after Nehru death.
evt-asuka-baekje-fall: A Tang-dynasty painting of the Baekje ambassador, captioned in Chinese text — a rare contemporary image of the kingdom whose destruction in 660 sent shockwaves across the Korean peninsula and all the way to Japan.
evt-sungkyunkwan: The Myeongnyundang lecture hall at Sungkyunkwan, the royal Confucian academy in Seoul.
evt-tumipampa-capital: The ruins of Pumapungo at Cuenca, Ecuador — the Inca city of Tumipampa, the empire northern capital.
evt-atahualpa-ransom: The Ransom Room (Cuarto del Rescate) at Cajamarca, where Atahualpa gold and silver ransom was gathered for Pizarro.
evt-venetian-trade-privileges: Southeastern Europe around 1000 — the Byzantine Balkans and Adriatic where Venice won its trade privileges.
evt-aksum-incense-trade: A satellite view of the Red Sea, the corridor along which Aksum carried frankincense and myrrh between Arabia and the Mediterranean.
evt-latin-american-independence-001: Charles III of Spain, the Bourbon king whose reforms tightened royal control over the colonies.
evt-latin-american-independence-119: A market scene in French Saint-Domingue, the Caribbean's richest sugar colony.
evt-latin-american-independence-028: Miguel Hidalgo, the priest whose rebel host was shattered at the Battle of Calderon Bridge.
evt-latin-american-independence-068: Agustin de Iturbide in imperial robes, crowned Emperor of the short-lived First Mexican Empire.
evt-latin-american-independence-072: King John VI acclaimed at Rio de Janeiro, now the seat of the Portuguese monarchy.
evt-latin-american-independence-031: A free man of color in revolutionary uniform, of the kind who filled both patriot and royalist armies.
evt-latin-american-independence-013: Toussaint Louverture, the general who led enslaved people to victory in the Haitian Revolution.
evt-latin-american-independence-018: The Portuguese royal family arrives in Brazil after fleeing Lisbon ahead of the French.
evt-latin-american-independence-073: King John VI of Portugal, who sailed home to Lisbon and left his son Pedro as regent in Brazil.
evt-latin-american-independence-026: Francisco de Miranda, leader of the short-lived First Venezuelan Republic.
evt-latin-american-independence-085: Jose Antonio Paez, the llanero hero who led Venezuela out of Gran Colombia and ruled it for decades.
evt-latin-american-independence-116: The death of Antonio Jose de Sucre, ambushed and shot in the mountains of southern Colombia.
evt-latin-american-independence-087: Jose de San Martin in old age, during his long, forgotten exile in Europe.
evt-latin-american-independence-075: Prince Pedro proclaims Brazil's independence at the Ipiranga brook, the Cry of Ipiranga.
evt-latin-american-independence-082: Simon Bolivar, who took dictatorial power in a bid to hold Gran Colombia together.
evt-latin-american-independence-086: Facundo Quiroga, an Argentine caudillo, the personalist strongman typical of the new republics.
evt-latin-american-independence-121: An engraving of the Tumult of Aranjuez, the mob seizing the minister Godoy and toppling Charles IV.
evt-latin-american-independence-024: The open cabildo of Buenos Aires during the May Revolution, deciding to remove the Spanish viceroy.
evt-latin-american-independence-056: The La Rotonda monument in Guayaquil, where San Martin and Bolivar met once behind closed doors.
evt-latin-american-independence-115: Priests bless the rebel banners of the 1817 Pernambucan Revolt against the crown in Rio.
evt-latin-american-independence-099: A naval clash of the War of the Pacific, the Esmeralda sinking at the Battle of Iquique.
evt-latin-american-independence-101: The handwritten Rio Branco Free Womb Law, freeing children born to enslaved mothers in Brazil.
evt-latin-american-independence-106: Cuban cavalry charging under Antonio Maceo in the last war for independence from Spain.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-005: A depiction of Africans seized in a raid to be sold into the slave trade — the violent capture at the trade’s African source, here at its earliest transatlantic reach to the Americas.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-006: A 16th-century Indigenous-drawn codex showing a Spanish encomendero assaulting an Indigenous laborer — a contemporary record of the violence of the encomienda system.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-010: Bartolomé de las Casas, the Dominican friar who argued at the Valladolid debate that Indigenous people were fully human and must not be enslaved.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-011: Frans Post's painting of a sugar mill (engenho) in Pernambuco, Brazil, with enslaved laborers in the foreground — the plantation economy that drove Brazil's sugar boom.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-018: Enslaved laborers cutting sugar cane on a Caribbean plantation, an overseer on horseback behind them — the brutal sugar economy that made islands like Barbados rich.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-031: A period watercolor of the slave ship Marie Séraphique, captives crowded along the deck — a vessel built to carry human beings as cargo.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-037: An early-19th-century view of the British slaving fort on Bunce Island in the Sierra Leone River, ships riding at anchor offshore.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-043: Enslaved laborers loading hogsheads of sugar for shipment on a Caribbean coast — the sugar wealth that made colonies like Saint-Domingue the richest on earth.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-058: The Battle of Vertières (1803), the decisive engagement of the Saint-Domingue revolution, in which the formerly enslaved army defeated the French.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-065: William Wilberforce, the parliamentary leader of the decades-long campaign that won Britain abolition of the slave trade in 1807.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-074: A contemporary 1831 woodcut of Nat Turner’s rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia — a sensational pro-slavery print made to stoke fear of revolt.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-076: The Wedgwood “Am I Not a Man and a Brother?” medallion, the emblem of the British abolition movement that pressed for the 1833 act ending slavery across most of the empire.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-095: The Memorial to the Abolition of Slavery in Nantes, the French port that outfitted more slave ships than any other.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-097: Marcus Garvey, the Pan-Africanist leader and founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association, in ceremonial dress in 1922.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-106: Agostino Brunias's painting of a West Indian market, depicting the mixed African and European Creole society of the colonial Caribbean.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-007: An engraving of the King of Kongo — the conventional period image of Afonso I, the Catholic ruler who protested the seizure of his free subjects.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-030: The Brookes diagram of a British slave ship, captives packed in rows below decks — the harrowing reality of the Middle Passage crossing.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-041: An 18th-century engraving of a slave revolt in Jamaica, taken to depict Tacky’s uprising of 1760–61.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-050: The Brookes broadside, showing enslaved Africans stowed in a slave ship — the abolition movement’s most widely reproduced image.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-060: A period print of the 1791 uprising in Saint-Domingue, the revolt that forced revolutionary France to abolish colonial slavery.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-062: The Battle of Palm Tree Hill in Saint-Domingue, where yellow fever and fierce resistance destroyed Napoleon’s expedition.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-075: Albert Duperly’s print of the burning of the Roehampton estate during the Baptist War, the 1831–32 Jamaica rebellion.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-081: Jean-Baptiste Debret's depiction of slavery in Brazil, an overseer with a whip — the institution Brazil kept long after halting the Atlantic trade.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-084: The manuscript of Brazil’s 1871 Law of the Free Womb (Lei do Ventre Livre), which declared children born to enslaved women free.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-089: A Gullah woman weaving a sweetgrass basket in Charleston, a craft carried from West and Central Africa to the Sea Islands.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-090: The Cecil Rhodes statue being removed from the University of Cape Town in 2015, part of a wider reckoning with the legacies of slavery and empire.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-091: A botanical illustration of sugar cane (Saccharum officinarum), the labor-hungry crop that drove the Atlantic trade.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-098: A reproduction of a 1769 Charleston handbill advertising the sale of enslaved Africans just landed from a slave ship — the trade reduced to commerce.
evt-atlantic-slave-trade-103: A 1738 indenture certificate binding Henry Mayer to years of service — the indentured labor that preceded hereditary racial slavery in the English colonies.
evt-age-of-exploration-005: A full-size replica of the caravel La Pinta — the small, nimble lateen-rigged ship that opened up the Atlantic coast.
evt-age-of-exploration-013: A period portrait long identified as King John II of Portugal, the spymaster prince who ran the push toward India.
evt-age-of-exploration-019: Brass mariner's astrolabes in a museum case at Lagos, Portugal — the ring sailors used to read the sun's height and find their latitude.
evt-age-of-exploration-032: An anonymous portrait of Vasco da Gama, the captain who rounded Africa and reached India by sea, wearing the cross of the Order of Christ.
evt-age-of-exploration-035: A devotional-panel detail of King Manuel I of Portugal at prayer, the monarch who presided over Portugal’s golden age of exploration.
evt-age-of-exploration-068: The printed title page of the New Laws of 1542, the royal code that tried to curb the encomienda and ban indigenous slavery.
evt-age-of-exploration-078: A silver eight-reales coin of Ferdinand and Isabella — the Spanish dollar, or piece of eight, that became the early-modern world’s money.
evt-age-of-exploration-096: An engraving of a King of Kongo (Manikongo), the title held by the Christian ruler Afonso I, who begged Portugal to stop the slavers bleeding his kingdom.
evt-age-of-exploration-097: A hand-colored lithograph of Queen Njinga (Nzinga Mbande) of Ndongo and Matamba, who outmaneuvered the Portuguese in Angola for decades.
evt-age-of-exploration-106: Bleeding, scorbutic gums caused by vitamin-C deficiency — the classic sign of scurvy, the disease that killed more sailors than storms.
evt-age-of-exploration-119: A wooden cross-staff, the cheap star-sighting instrument a sailor slid along a crosspiece to read his latitude.
evt-age-of-exploration-142: A 1683 engraving of a Portuguese galleon, the big, heavily gunned ship that hauled the Atlantic treasure fleets and the Pacific run.
evt-age-of-exploration-026: A carved-stone Taíno zemi, a three-pointed religious object of the Caribbean people Columbus met across the Greater Antilles.
evt-age-of-exploration-028: A portrait of Pope Alexander VI, who issued the Inter caetera papal bulls handing Spain dominion over the lands Columbus had found.
evt-age-of-exploration-031: A page from the Codex Kingsborough showing a Spanish encomendero abusing an indigenous man — a contemporary protest against the encomienda.
evt-age-of-exploration-059: A mural of the meeting between the Spanish and the Tlaxcala, the indigenous nation whose warriors made the conquest of the Aztecs possible.
evt-age-of-exploration-069: A portrait of Fray Bartolomé de las Casas, who argued at the Valladolid debate that indigenous Americans were rational humans with rights.
evt-age-of-exploration-073: A portrait of Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Society of Jesus — the Jesuits, spearhead of Catholic missionary expansion.
evt-age-of-exploration-088: A painting of Samuel de Champlain arriving at Quebec, greeted by indigenous canoes — the founding moment of New France and its fur trade.
evt-age-of-exploration-094: Auguste Biard’s painting of captive Africans being branded and loaded onto a slave ship — the Atlantic slave trade at full industrial scale.
evt-age-of-exploration-103: The Toruń portrait of Nicolaus Copernicus, who published the claim that the Earth circles the sun.
evt-age-of-exploration-107: A field of growing tobacco plants — the American crop that became the cash plant that saved Virginia and the era’s first global craze.
evt-age-of-exploration-108: A circa-1590 painting of the Manila galleon met by Chamorro canoes in the Pacific — the ship that bridged the last ocean and linked the continents.
evt-age-of-exploration-121: The Fortaleza Ozama, the oldest surviving European fortress in the Americas, built at Santo Domingo on Hispaniola.
evt-age-of-exploration-130: A painting of the Spaniards’ first interview with Atahualpa’s people at Cajamarca, the meeting that turned into the ambush of the Inca emperor.
evt-age-of-exploration-131: The jungle-buried stone ruins of Espíritu Pampa, the site of Vilcabamba, the last refuge of the Neo-Inca State.
evt-age-of-exploration-133: A Spanish colonial silver eight-reales coin struck at the Potosí mint — the New World silver the crown skimmed with its royal fifth.
evt-age-of-exploration-143: A 16th-century painting of the port of Seville, crammed with shipping — the single harbor where Spain’s escorted treasure fleets unloaded their silver.
evt-age-of-exploration-030: A diagram of the Columbian Exchange, tracing the crops, animals, and diseases that crossed between the Old World and the New.
evt-age-of-exploration-066: Potosí beneath the silver mountain of Cerro Rico — the mines the mita labor draft fed with conscripted Andean villagers.
evt-age-of-exploration-099: Ears of maize — the New World grain whose spread across the Old World was one of the great crop transfers of the Columbian Exchange.
evt-dido-founds-carthage: Dido illustrated in the Vergilius Vaticanus, a late-Roman illuminated manuscript of Virgil's Aeneid (c. 400 CE) — the kind of source through which the West remembers her.
evt-byrsa-hill: Excavated foundations of Punic houses on Byrsa hill, with a surviving storage jar and cisterns set among the courtyard walls.
evt-tophet-sanctuary: Carved votive stelae standing in the Tophet precinct at Carthage, the kind of markers that crowned the buried urns.
evt-baal-hammon-worship: Terracotta statue of Baal Hammon enthroned, bearded and flanked by winged sphinxes (Thinissut sanctuary, Bardo National Museum, Tunis).
evt-tanit-ascendancy: A Punic votive stele carved with the classic "sign of Tanit" — a triangle topped by a horizontal bar and a disc — the emblem of Carthage's chief goddess.
evt-melqart-cult-carthage: Stele showing the god Melqart, striding above a lion — the Phoenician patron deity of Tyre whose cult Carthage carried west.
evt-punic-script: Bilingual dedication at the theater of Leptis Magna, Libya — Latin above, Neo-Punic below — showing the script still in use under Roman rule.
evt-carthage-walls: Museum reconstruction painting of Carthage, showing the walled peninsula and the ringed military harbor that the great fortifications enclosed.
evt-carthage-early-trade: Carthaginian silver coin (tetradrachm) carrying the head of the goddess Tanit — struck from the silver wealth that flowed through Carthage's trade.
evt-carthage-sardinia: The seaside ruins of Tharros on Sardinia's west coast, one of the Phoenician-founded ports Carthage took over.
evt-carthage-shipbuilding: The reconstructed remains of the Punic warship recovered off Marsala, Sicily — the actual archaeological proof of Carthage's prefab shipbuilding.
evt-battle-himera-480: Giuseppe Sciuti's 19th-century painting of the rout at Himera, with Hamilcar's sacrificial fire blazing at left.
evt-aristotle-constitution: Marble bust of Aristotle (Roman copy after a Greek original), Palazzo Altemps, Rome.
evt-african-territorial-empire: The reach of Carthage's empire (English-labeled map), with the North African heartland anchoring its territory and colonies.
evt-gold-trade-west-africa: A Carthaginian gold stater (c. 350–320 BCE): the goddess Tanit wreathed in grain on one face, the Punic horse on the other.
evt-sacred-band-carthage: A gilded Carthaginian breastplate from Ksour es-Saf (Bardo Museum, Tunis) — the kind of splendid armor that marked out Carthage's aristocratic soldiers.
evt-agathocles-invasion: Gold coin of Agathocles of Syracuse: helmeted Athena on one side, a winged thunderbolt and griffin with his royal title on the other.
evt-cothon-harbor: A 1958 aerial photograph of the ancient Punic harbor basins at Carthage, showing the circular naval cothon and the rectangular merchant harbor that made Carthage the commercial master of the western Mediterranean.
evt-kerkouane: A pink-plaster Punic bathtub still set in its house at Kerkouane — the kind of in-home bathing that surprised excavators.
evt-grain-exports: Excavated Punic-quarter ruins on Byrsa Hill at Carthage, with the city and the sea beyond — the metropolis that the African grain lands fed.
evt-first-punic-war-begins: A row of bronze Carthaginian and Roman warship rams, recovered from the waters off Sicily and shown together in a museum case — the surviving hardware of the long sea war that opened in 264 BCE.
evt-siege-agrigentum: The Temple of Concordia at Agrigento — surviving ruins of the rich Greek city Rome stormed and emptied in 261 BCE.
evt-battle-mylae: Bronze warship rams of the kind torn from captured Punic ships to decorate Rome's victory columns.
evt-battle-ecnomus: A recovered bronze ram, the business end of the warships that fought one of antiquity's largest sea battles.
evt-hamilcar-barca-sicily: A Punic gilded bronze cuirass — the kind of armor a Carthaginian commander's force carried into the field.
evt-battle-aegates-islands: A bronze warship ram raised from the seabed off the Aegates Islands, its socket cast with a relief of a winged Victory — one of the rams torn from the fleets sunk in the battle of 241 BCE.
evt-mercenary-war: A silver shekel struck by the rebels, its Greek legend ΛΙΒΥΩΝ proclaiming a breakaway "state of the Libyans."
evt-hamilcar-barca-spain: Benjamin West's painting of the legendary scene: Hamilcar holds young Hannibal at the altar to swear eternal enmity against Rome.
evt-hasdrubal-fair: Modern bust monument to Hasdrubal the Fair at Cartagena (ancient New Carthage), the Spanish city he founded around 228 BC as the Barcid family's silver-rich headquarters on the Iberian peninsula.
evt-new-carthage-silver: A Barcid silver quarter-shekel minted at Carthago Nova — a wreathed head on the front, a war elephant on the back, struck from the local mines.
evt-hannibal-takes-command: Hannibal Barca rendered as a battle-hardened commander, the Carthaginian general who took charge of the army in Spain at twenty-six.
evt-siege-saguntum: The hilltop fortress of Sagunto, Spain — the long acropolis where the besieged townspeople made their last stand.
evt-crossing-alps: Heinrich Leutemann's illustration of the army struggling over the Alps, war elephants and all.
evt-battle-trebia: Bust traditionally identified as Hannibal Barca, the Carthaginian general who won his first Italian victory at the Trebia.
evt-battle-trasimene: Lake Trasimene and the wooded hills along the northern shore, where Hannibal concealed his entire army for the ambush.
evt-battle-cannae: The Death of Paulus Aemilius at Cannae (216 BC), depicting the moment Rome suffered its worst-ever battlefield defeat as Hannibal's double-envelopment destroyed two consular armies in a single afternoon.
evt-scipio-africanus: The Continence of Scipio, a celebrated scene in which the young Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio returns a captured noblewoman to her Iberian family — the act of restraint that won him allied support and turned the war in Spain.
evt-hannibal-exile: Marble bust traditionally identified as Hannibal Barca, who died in exile rather than fall into Roman hands.
evt-numidian-cavalry: Numidian bronze coin of King Masinissa: a royal portrait on one face, a galloping horse — the Numidians' famous mount — on the other.
evt-war-elephants: Terracotta statuette of a war elephant carrying a fighting tower and rider, from Pompeii.
evt-religious-syncretism: A terracotta incense-burner shaped as the head of Baal Hammon, the bearded chief god of Carthage, crowned with a feathered headdress.
evt-purple-dye-production: Shells of the spiny dye-murex, the Mediterranean sea snail whose mucus gland yielded Tyrian purple.
evt-carthage-coinage: A silver Carthaginian tetradrachm (c. 350-320 BCE) showing the head of the goddess Tanit, the signature Punic coin portrait.
evt-balearic-slingers: Ancient sling-stones of the kind hurled by Balearic slingers, shaped to fly straight and hit hard.
evt-terence-playwright: The medieval manuscript portrait of Terence (Vatican Library, Vat. lat. 3868), the standard image of the playwright.
evt-punic-inscriptions: A Punic votive stele carved with a cultic scene and an inscription in the Punic alphabet, the kind of stone that fills the tophets.
evt-cato-delenda-est: A gaunt, hard-faced Roman marble bust traditionally identified as Cato the Elder, carved in the unflattering 'veristic' style that prized every wrinkle as proof of character.
evt-third-punic-war-begins: A museum case of Third Punic War relics from the siege — a corroded iron sword, lead sling-bullets, and a heavy stone catapult ball, the everyday hardware of the final defense.
evt-destruction-carthage: Edward Poynter's Catapulta (1868) imagines Roman siege crews at work beneath the walls of Carthage in 146 BC — the board propped against the machine reads the Senate's decree: Delenda est Carthago.
evt-punic-literature-lost: A Punic limestone stele incised with rows of the Carthaginian alphabet — votive and funerary stones like this are nearly all the written Punic that survives, since the literature itself is gone.
evt-carthage-economic-recovery: A Carthaginian silver double shekel of roughly 160–149 BCE: the goddess Tanit on the front, a horse on the back — coinage from the very decades the city's wealth alarmed Rome.
evt-temple-eshmun-carthage: The summit of the Byrsa hill at Carthage, scattered with column capitals and ruins beneath the old Acropolium — the high point of the city where the great temple of Eshmun once stood.
evt-mago-dynasty-founded: A Carthaginian silver tetradrachm of the Magonid era, its reverse stamped with the date palm — the city's punning emblem (the Greek for palm, phoinix, also meant Phoenician).
evt-battle-alalia: A map of the Battle of Alalia (535 BC) showing the Carthaginian and Etruscan domains that closed ranks to drive the Phocaean Greeks from Corsica and divide the western Mediterranean between them.
evt-malchus-campaigns: The Punic ruins of Motya, the Carthaginian island-stronghold off western Sicily — the kind of foothold Malchus fought to hold.
evt-carthage-iberian-expansion: A terracotta figure of the goddess Tanit from the Es Cuieram cave shrine on Ibiza — a Punic offering left in Carthage's western colonies.
evt-hanno-great-expedition: A Carthaginian silver dekadrachm, its reverse showing the winged horse Pegasos — coinage from the seafaring city that sent Hanno down the African coast.
evt-himilco-atlantic: A Carthaginian silver tetradrachm with a lion before a date palm — money from the trading power whose captains, like Himilco, probed the Atlantic tin routes.
evt-treaty-rome-509: A marble portrait head of the Greek historian Polybius, the sole ancient source who preserved the text of the first Rome–Carthage treaty.
evt-hamilcar-i: A Carthaginian silver tetradrachm showing a horse crowned by a winged Victory — coinage of the Magonid age that produced commanders like Hamilcar I.
evt-battle-crimissus: A Greek hoplite's bronze panoply — Corinthian helmet, breastplate, greaves and spear. Timoleon's heavily-armored Greeks cut down the Carthaginian army on the Crimissus in 341 BCE.
evt-hannibal-mago-himera-revenge: The ruins of Himera in Sicily. Hannibal Mago stormed and razed the Greek city in 409 BCE, avenging his grandfather's defeat there seventy years before.
evt-treaty-inscriptions: The Cippus of Melqart, a marble monument carrying a bilingual Punic-and-Greek inscription. Carthage cut its solemn agreements into stone and bronze like this; the Rome treaties survive only because Polybius copied them.
evt-carthage-suffetes: A Punic votive stele with a carved hand above lines of Punic script. Carthage's records were written in this alphabet, including the dedications that name its suffetes — the two chief magistrates the city elected each year.
evt-bomilcar-coup: A Siculo-Punic silver tetradrachm of around 320–300 BCE — a lion before a date palm, with a Punic legend below. Carthage struck coins like this in the very years Bomilcar tried and failed to seize the city.
evt-sicilian-wars-continue: The Euryalus fortress, anchor of the great Dionysian walls of Syracuse. It was the city's stubborn defenses that broke Himilco's Carthaginian siege of 397 BCE.
evt-su-october-revolution: Armed Red Guards of the Vulkan factory pose with rifles and machine guns beneath their unit banner in 1917 Petrograd.
evt-su-gulag-system: A watchtower and turf-roofed barrack at a camp in the Vorkuta complex, one of the Arctic coal-mining hubs of the Gulag.
evt-su-great-purge: A page of NKVD Order No. 00447, stamped "top secret" and dated 30 July 1937 — the quota order that set the Terror's machinery running.
evt-su-gulag-archipelago: Cover of an English-language edition of The Gulag Archipelago.
evt-su-holodomor: Kharkiv, 1933: famine victims collapsed on a city street as a passerby walks on — one of Alexander Wienerberger's smuggled photographs.
evt-su-ussr-founded: The bound cover of the 1922 Declaration and Treaty establishing the USSR, dated Moscow, 30 December 1922.
evt-su-february-revolution: A vast crowd packs Znamenskaya Square in Petrograd during the February Revolution of 1917, gathered at the foot of the equestrian statue of Alexander III.
evt-su-lenin-april-theses: Lenin photographed in 1917, clean-shaven and in a worker's cap for the false identity papers he used while dodging arrest that summer.
evt-su-july-days: Crowds scatter across Petrograd's Nevsky Prospekt as troops open fire during the July Days, July 1917.
evt-su-kornilov-affair: General Lavr Kornilov is carried shoulder-high by admirers in 1917, near the peak of his standing as the army's commander-in-chief.
evt-su-storming-winter-palace: Soldiers and Red Guards crowd outside the Winter Palace just after its capture, 26 October 1917.
evt-su-decree-on-peace-land: The front page of Izvestia carrying the Decree on Land, dated 26 October 1917, in the old Russian orthography.
evt-su-constituent-assembly: The Constituent Assembly in session in the Tauride Palace, Petrograd, on its single day, 18 January 1918.
evt-su-lenin: Lenin addresses a crowd in 1919, in winter coat and cap, at the height of his power as head of the Soviet state.
evt-su-treaty-brest-litovsk: The Russian delegation arrives at Brest-Litovsk, greeted beside the train by German officers in spiked Pickelhaube helmets, early 1918.
evt-su-czech-legion: Czechoslovak Legion troops drawn up in formation with their band, Vladivostok, 1918.
evt-su-allied-intervention: American troops march behind the Stars and Stripes through Vladivostok, 1918.
evt-su-red-army-founded: Trotsky, arms spread, addresses troops from atop an armored vehicle painted "Watchman of the Revolution" and marked with the Red Star, 1920.
evt-su-cheka-founded: Felix Dzerzhinsky, the founding head of the Cheka, in a studio portrait.
evt-su-red-terror: A Petrograd crowd holds a banner reading "Death to the bourgeoisie and its lackeys — Long live the Red Terror!", 1918.
evt-su-romanov-execution: The Romanov family in 1913: Nicholas II and Alexandra with their daughters and the heir Alexei — all murdered five years later.
evt-su-war-communism: Armed Red detachments haul off a peasant family's grain — a watercolor by Ivan Vladimirov, an eyewitness painter of the period.
evt-su-polish-soviet-war: Polish infantry on the march during the Battle of Warsaw, August 1920 — the "Miracle on the Vistula."
evt-su-makhno-greens: Nestor Makhno (seated, leather jacket) with the commanders of his anarchist Black Army, Berdyansk, 1919.
evt-su-white-defeat-crimea: The White evacuation fleet steams out of Crimea in November 1920, carrying tens of thousands into exile.
evt-su-kronstadt: Red Army troops advancing across the frozen Gulf of Finland to storm the Kronstadt fortress, March 1921.
evt-su-tambov-rebellion: Commanders of the Tambov 'Green' peasant army, around 1920.
evt-su-nep: A 1920s drawing of "NEPmen" — the well-dressed private traders the New Economic Policy briefly allowed back into Soviet life.
evt-su-ban-on-factions: Delegates of the Tenth Party Congress of 1921, which passed both the NEP and the ban on factions.
evt-su-zinoviev-letter: Alexandra Kollontai, the leading voice of the Workers' Opposition.
evt-su-russian-famine-1921: Bodies of famine victims gathered at a cemetery during the Russian famine of 1921.
evt-su-american-relief-administration: A Russian-language ARA relief poster crediting 'the gift of the American people' and Herbert Hoover.
evt-su-stalin-gensec: Joseph Stalin around 1920, shortly before he became General Secretary.
evt-su-lenin-testament: Vladimir Lenin around 1920, before the strokes that ended his career.
evt-su-lenin-death: Stalin (left) with Kamenev and Tomsky carrying Lenin's coffin, January 1924.
evt-su-stalin-rise: Stalin (left) strolls with Rykov, Kamenev, and Zinoviev in 1925. Within four years he would politically destroy all three.
evt-su-united-opposition: Trotsky (left, in fur hat) with Kamenev and Zinoviev in the mid-1920s, the trio who briefly united against Stalin.
evt-su-trotsky-exile: Trotsky in 1928, photographed during his internal exile before Stalin expelled him from the USSR altogether.
evt-su-trotsky-assassination: Trotsky (center) with American supporters in Mexico, photographed in 1940, the year an assassin reached him.
evt-su-bukharin-fall: Nikolai Bukharin, the Party's star theorist and leader of the doomed "Right Opposition."
evt-su-socialism-one-country: Stalin in the 1920s, when he formulated "Socialism in One Country" as both doctrine and political weapon.
evt-su-stalin-cult: Marchers carry rows of identical Stalin portraits, the manufactured cult of personality made visible.
evt-su-collectivization: Komsomol activists dig up grain that peasants had hidden in a village cemetery during the collectivization drive.
evt-su-dekulakization: Women deported as "kulaks" in 1930, set to clearing forest at a remote special settlement.
evt-su-soviet-famine-1932: A 1933 map of the USSR with the worst famine zones inked in black — Ukraine, the Volga, the North Caucasus, and the Kazakh lands.
evt-su-kazakh-famine: A memorial stone to the victims of the 1931–1933 Kazakh famine (Asharshylyk), inscribed in Kazakh and Russian.
evt-su-raphael-lemkin-genocide: Raphael Lemkin, the jurist who coined the word "genocide" and drove the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
evt-su-five-year-plan: Yakov Guminer's 1931 poster: '2 + 2 = 5' — the arithmetic of over-fulfilling the Five-Year Plan through worker enthusiasm.
evt-su-gosplan: A 1920s organizational chart of the Soviet planning apparatus, with Gosplan (ГОСПЛАН) at the hub directing the republics' economies.
evt-su-electrification-goelro: A propaganda poster of Lenin spreading a wave of light over a map of Russia, beneath his slogan that communism equals Soviet power plus electrification.
evt-su-magnitogorsk: The Magnitogorsk steel works under construction in the 1930s, smokestacks rising from the bare Ural steppe.
evt-su-dnieper-dam: The Dnieper Hydroelectric Dam under construction around 1930, its sweeping curved spillway taking shape across the river.
evt-su-white-sea-canal: A construction-era poster addressed to the canal's prisoner-laborers ('kanaloarmeets'), telling them hot work shrinks your sentence.
evt-su-second-five-year-plan: The assembly line of the Stalingrad Tractor Factory in 1930, workers fitting together tractors on one of the showpiece new plants.
evt-su-stakhanovite: Alexei Stakhanov, the coal miner whose staged record shift became the face of the Soviet cult of the heroic worker.
evt-su-likbez-literacy: A literacy-campaign poster — 'Woman! Learn to read!' — showing a child reading while a peasant mother looks on.
evt-su-kgb-founded: Preserved KGB prison cells, now a museum in Tartu, Estonia — the heavy doors and corridor of a Soviet security-police lockup.
evt-su-kirov-murder: Sergei Kirov in 1934, the year he was assassinated — the murder that became Stalin's excuse for the Terror.
evt-su-moscow-trials: Nikolai Bukharin's NKVD arrest photograph — the revolution's leading theorist, soon to confess and be shot in the 1938 show trial.
evt-su-army-purge: The five first Marshals of the Soviet Union, 1935. Three of them — including Tukhachevsky (seated, far left) — were shot in the purge of the army.
evt-su-yezhovshchina: Stalin and Molotov by the canal — the doctored version. Yezhov, once standing at the right, has been erased and replaced with water after his fall.
evt-su-orthodox-church: A 1930 Soviet poster announcing a public mass burning of religious icons, with a band to play.
evt-su-league-militant-godless: The October 1930 cover of 'Bezbozhnik' ('The Godless'), the League's magazine, caricaturing a priest to mock religion.
evt-su-cathedral-christ-saviour: The Cathedral of Christ the Saviour shrouded in smoke as it is dynamited in Moscow, December 1931.
evt-su-palace-soviets: A 1937 Soviet stamp showing the planned Palace of the Soviets, its tower crowned by the giant statue of Lenin.
evt-su-women-zhenotdel: Women gather for an early Zhenotdel meeting in 1920, beneath Soviet banners.
evt-su-korenizatsiya: The 1930 Latin alphabet devised for Moksha, one of dozens of Soviet languages given a written form under korenizatsiya.
evt-su-socialist-realism: Isaak Brodsky's painting of a mass rally under red banners, a textbook example of Socialist Realism.
evt-su-gorky-socialist-realism: Maxim Gorky, the novelist installed as figurehead of the Union of Soviet Writers.
evt-su-mayakovsky-death: Vladimir Mayakovsky as a young Futurist poet, around 1910.
evt-su-akhmatova-mandelstam: Osip Mandelstam's NKVD arrest photograph, taken after his 1938 detention; he died in a transit camp that year.
evt-su-shostakovich-5th: Dmitri Shostakovich in his trademark round glasses, around the time of the Fifth Symphony.
evt-su-pioneers-komsomol: A Komsomol assignment voucher ('putyovka'), the document that directed young members to work and study placements.
evt-su-soviet-healthcare: Nikolai Semashko, the first Soviet health commissar, whose name the universal health system carried.
evt-su-comintern-founded: Delegates at the first Comintern congress in Moscow, 1919, under a banner reading "Workers of all countries, unite!"
evt-su-spanish-civil-war-aid: Republican pilots eat beside a Soviet-supplied Polikarpov I-16 fighter, the most modern aircraft the USSR sent to Spain.
evt-su-international-brigades: International Brigade volunteers in Spain, 1937, the foreign antifascists who came to fight for the Republic.
evt-su-khalkhin-gol: Camouflaged Soviet tanks on the Mongolian steppe during the 1939 battle of Khalkhin Gol.
evt-su-molotov-ribbentrop: Stalin shakes hands with German foreign minister Joachim von Ribbentrop in the Kremlin, August 1939.
evt-su-poland-partition-1939: German and Soviet officers together in occupied Poland, September 1939, as the two powers partitioned the country.
evt-su-baltic-annexation: Red Army troops march past a Lithuanian border marker as the USSR occupies the Baltic states, 1940.
evt-su-katyn-massacre: A mass grave of murdered Polish officers in the Katyn forest, uncovered in 1943.
evt-su-winter-war: A Finnish soldier in white winter camouflage aims a rifle in the snow during the Winter War.
evt-su-barbarossa: German troops crossing the Soviet frontier on 22 June 1941, a burning village on the horizon, at the opening of Operation Barbarossa.
evt-su-hunger-plan: Herbert Backe, the Nazi agriculture official who drafted the Hunger Plan, at his desk.
evt-su-soviet-pow-deaths: Thousands of Soviet prisoners crowded into an open-air German holding pen, 1941 — the kind of camp where most died of starvation and cold that winter.
evt-su-industry-evacuation: The Chelyabinsk tractor plant in the 1930s, with rows of tracked tractors outside — the deep-interior factory that absorbed evacuated industry and became wartime 'Tankograd.'
evt-su-siege-leningrad: Bundled-up Leningraders drawing water from a broken main on a frozen, snow-choked Nevsky Prospekt during the siege.
evt-su-battle-moscow: Siberian soldiers in winter caps riding a freight train west to defend Moscow in 1941, one playing an accordion — the fresh divisions that helped turn the battle.
evt-su-richard-sorge: Richard Sorge, the Soviet spy who operated in Tokyo under cover as a German journalist.
evt-su-zhukov: Marshal Georgy Zhukov in dress uniform, his chest covered in decorations — the war's emblematic Soviet commander.
evt-su-stalingrad: Soviet infantry storm across the rubble of Stalingrad, the gutted shells of the city's buildings smoking behind them.
evt-su-order-227: The first page of the original Order No. 227, headed "Not for publication" and dated 28 July 1942, Moscow.
evt-su-kursk: Soviet infantry advance behind T-34 tanks through the smoke of the Voronezh Front during the Battle of Kursk, July 1943.
evt-su-operation-bagration: Soviet troops march through liberated Polotsk in Belarus past a banner reading "Polotsk is ours — onward to the West," July 1944.
evt-su-red-army-rape-1945: A column of German refugee carts (a Flüchtlingstreck) flees East Prussia ahead of the advancing Red Army, winter 1944–45.
evt-su-berlin-captured: Yevgeny Khaldei's "Raising a Flag over the Reichstag," the staged and retouched image of a Soviet soldier hoisting the red banner over a shattered Berlin, May 1945.
evt-su-soviet-japan-war: Soviet troops march into the Manchurian city of Harbin as crowds line the street, August 1945.
evt-su-great-patriotic-war-cost: Soviet civilians carry their belongings through a burning, ruined street — about two-thirds of the USSR's war dead were civilians.
evt-su-repatriation-1945: A 14-year-old Ukrainian forced laborer (Ostarbeiter) at a workbench in Germany — returnees like him were screened as suspect traitors at war's end.
evt-su-yalta-conference: The Big Three at Yalta, February 1945: Churchill, a visibly ailing Roosevelt, and Stalin seated together in the palace courtyard.
evt-su-potsdam-conference: Attlee, Truman, and Stalin seated in wicker chairs at Potsdam, July 1945 — a different lineup from Yalta five months earlier.
evt-su-iron-curtain: A preserved stretch of the real Iron Curtain near Čížov in the Czech Republic: barbed-wire fence, concrete tank traps, and a watchtower.
evt-su-comecon: The former COMECON headquarters in Moscow, its distinctive "open book" tower still standing decades after the bloc dissolved.
evt-su-warsaw-pact: Warsaw Pact leaders lined up at a 1987 summit in East Berlin, Gorbachev at center among the bloc's heads of state.
evt-su-berlin-blockade: Berliners watch an airlift plane come in to land at Tempelhof in 1948, a boy clambering up a lamppost for a better view.
evt-su-nuclear-bomb: A museum replica of RDS-1, the first Soviet atomic bomb — a close copy of the American "Fat Man" design.
evt-su-tito-split: Josip Broz Tito in his marshal's uniform — the Communist leader who defied Stalin and got away with it.
evt-su-zhdanovshchina: A 1948 Soviet postage stamp memorializing Andrei Zhdanov, the cultural enforcer who gave the crackdown its name.
evt-su-lysenko: Trofim Lysenko, the agronomist whose pseudoscience became official Soviet biology and wrecked the field for decades.
evt-su-jewish-antifascist-committee: Committee leaders Itzik Feffer (left) and Solomon Mikhoels (right) with Albert Einstein during their 1943 US fundraising tour; both were later killed.
evt-su-doctors-plot: The April 1953 Soviet press announcement, weeks after Stalin's death, declaring the arrested doctors innocent and rehabilitated — and naming each of them.
evt-su-stalin-death: Stalin's flag-draped casket on a gun carriage, escorted by ranks of soldiers through Moscow during the March 1953 state funeral.
evt-su-beria-fall: Lavrenty Beria in NKVD uniform with his trademark pince-nez. The secret-police chief was arrested and shot in 1953.
evt-su-khrushchev: Nikita Khrushchev around 1962, wearing his characteristic half-smile.
evt-su-secret-speech: The first printed edition of the Secret Speech, a Polish "for party use only" pamphlet, Warsaw, March 1956.
evt-su-gulag-released: The preserved Perm-36 labor camp: barbed wire, wooden fences, and a guard tower of the kind dismantled across the Gulag after 1953.
evt-su-gulag-literature: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, the former camp prisoner whose novella first named the Gulag in print.
evt-su-novy-mir: The masthead of Novy Mir ("New World"), the literary journal Tvardovsky steered through the Thaw.
evt-su-poznan-1956: Wladyslaw Gomulka addressing a vast crowd in Warsaw during the Polish October, 1956.
evt-su-hungarian-revolt: A burning Soviet armored carrier on a smoke-filled Budapest street during the 1956 fighting.
evt-su-thaw-literature: Ilya Ehrenburg, the writer whose 1954 novel gave the Thaw its name.
evt-su-sputnik: A full-size replica of Sputnik 1, the beach-ball-sized polished sphere with four trailing antennas that became the first object in orbit.
evt-su-laika: Laika, the Moscow stray chosen as the first animal to orbit Earth, photographed in 1957 before the flight.
evt-su-luna-2: The Luna 1/2 spacecraft: a sphere bristling with antennas, the design that became the first craft to reach the Moon.
evt-su-gagarin: Yuri Gagarin in uniform, weighed down with medals after becoming the first human in space — the smiling face the USSR put before the world.
evt-su-tereshkova: Valentina Tereshkova photographed in January 1963, months before she became the first woman to fly in space.
evt-su-korolev: A young Sergei Korolev in flying helmet and goggles (1929), years before the Gulag and his secret career as the USSR's Chief Designer.
evt-su-n1-rocket-failure: The towering N1 Moon rocket on its launch pad at Baikonur — the booster that failed all four times it flew.
evt-su-cosmonaut-deaths: The scorched, flattened wreckage of Soyuz 1 after its parachutes failed and the capsule hit the ground, killing Vladimir Komarov.
evt-su-novocherkassk: Crowds of striking workers gathered in Novocherkassk on 1 June 1962, the day before troops fired on the protest.
evt-su-berlin-wall-built: East German crews building up the Berlin Wall in late 1961, the barrier that sealed off West Berlin.
evt-su-cuban-missile-crisis: The U-2 spy-plane photograph of a Soviet medium-range missile site under construction in Cuba, 14 October 1962 — the image that opened the crisis.
evt-su-test-ban-treaty: President Kennedy signs the Partial Test Ban Treaty on 7 October 1963, the superpower pact halting nuclear tests in the atmosphere, space, and underwater.
evt-su-tsar-bomba: The fireball of the Tsar Bomba rising over Novaya Zemlya in 1961 — the largest nuclear explosion ever set off.
evt-su-sino-soviet-split: Mao Zedong and Nikita Khrushchev sitting together in Beijing in 1958, smiling — years before their alliance collapsed into rivalry.
evt-su-virgin-lands: A Soviet stamp block celebrating the Virgin Lands campaign, showing a tractor, ripe wheat, and the commemorative "Tselina" medal.
evt-su-khrushchev-ouster: Nikita Khrushchev in 1964, the year fellow Presidium members ousted him in a bloodless Kremlin coup.
evt-su-brezhnev: Leonid Brezhnev, who led the Soviet Union from 1964 to 1982 — the long, stable, slowly decaying era his successors named the Stagnation.
evt-su-kosygin-reform: The front page of Pravda, September 1965, announcing the decree 'On improving the management of industry' — the launch of the Kosygin reform.
evt-su-soviet-oil-windfall: Soviet (later Russian) oil output in millions of barrels per day: the steep 1970s climb that bankrolled the Brezhnev era, and the crash that followed.
evt-su-grain-imports: An American wheat field with grain silos — the kind of harvest the Soviet Union secretly bought up by the millions of tons in 1972.
evt-su-prague-spring: Crowds of Czechs surround Soviet tanks in the streets of Prague during the August 1968 invasion that ended the Prague Spring.
evt-su-brezhnev-doctrine: A burning Soviet tank in Prague, August 1968 — the invasion that the Brezhnev Doctrine was written to justify.
evt-su-eurocommunism: Enrico Berlinguer, leader of the Italian Communist Party and the chief architect of Eurocommunism, photographed in 1976.
evt-su-ussuri-clash: Soviet patrol boats on the Ussuri River during the 1969 border clashes with China.
evt-su-salt-i: Nixon and Brezhnev sign the SALT I and ABM agreements in Moscow, 1972 — the high-water mark of superpower détente.
evt-su-apollo-soyuz: American and Soviet commanders Thomas Stafford and Alexei Leonov shake hands in the docking hatch linking Apollo and Soyuz, July 1975.
evt-su-helsinki-accords: Western leaders sign the Helsinki Final Act in 1975, each at a nameplated national desk.
evt-su-1977-constitution: A 1977 Soviet souvenir stamp sheet marking the new Constitution — the red Constitution book and a medalled portrait of Brezhnev who signed it.
evt-su-khrushchyovka: A classic five-storey Khrushchyovka apartment block in Tomsk, Siberia — the cramped but private flats that rehoused millions of Soviet families.
evt-su-samizdat: Confiscated samizdat: hand-typed manuscripts and photo negatives of banned books, spread out after a search.
evt-su-vysotsky: Vladimir Vysotsky, the bard whose taped, never-officially-released songs spread across the USSR.
evt-su-sinyavsky-daniel: Andrei Sinyavsky, one of the two writers whose 1966 trial galvanized the dissident movement.
evt-su-chronicle-current-events: A typed samizdat page of the Chronicle of Current Events (Issue 22, November 1971), opening with a quote from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
evt-su-helsinki-watch: Yuri Orlov, the physicist who founded the Moscow Helsinki Group in 1976.
evt-su-solzhenitsyn-expelled: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn in the West in 1974, soon after being stripped of citizenship and deported from the Soviet Union.
evt-su-sakharov-exile: Andrei Sakharov mobbed by reporters, the bomb physicist who became the regime's best-known internal critic.
evt-su-sakharov-nobel: A 1991 Soviet stamp honoring Andrei Sakharov as a Nobel laureate — the recognition the USSR refused to let him collect in person in 1975, when his wife Elena Bonner read his Peace Prize lecture in Oslo.
evt-su-psychiatry-abuse: The Serbsky Institute in Moscow, the central institution where dissidents were evaluated and declared mentally ill.
evt-su-jewish-emigration: Refuseniks demonstrate outside the Soviet interior ministry in 1973, holding hand-lettered signs demanding exit visas.
evt-su-afghanistan: A Soviet soldier takes cover with his rifle inside a bombed-out building during the war in Afghanistan.
evt-su-olympics-1980: Marathon runners pass St Basil's Cathedral on Red Square during the 1980 Moscow Olympics.
evt-su-detente-collapse: A U.S. Pershing II missile on its launcher — the fast, accurate weapon NATO deployed in Europe as détente collapsed.
evt-su-sdi-pressure: Artist's concept of an SDI "Star Wars" battle station firing laser beams at Soviet warheads in orbit.
evt-su-kal-007: The Korean Air Lines Boeing 747, registration HL7442 — the actual aircraft later shot down as Flight 007 — taking off in 1980.
evt-su-able-archer: President Reagan meets Oleg Gordievsky, the KGB officer-turned-British-spy whose warnings exposed the Soviet Able Archer panic.
evt-su-brezhnev-death: Leonid Brezhnev's grave and bust in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis, where he was buried after his death in November 1982.
evt-su-andropov: Official portrait of Yuri Andropov, the former KGB chief who led the USSR for fifteen months before his death in 1984.
evt-su-chernenko: Konstantin Chernenko, the ailing Brezhnev-era apparatchik whose brief rule capped the Soviet gerontocracy.
evt-su-gorbachev-elected: Mikhail Gorbachev, who became General Secretary in 1985 as the youngest member of the leadership.
evt-su-anti-alcohol: A 1985 Soviet stamp, "Sobriety is the norm of life," showing a wholesome family with the cinema, museum and theatre instead of the bottle, propaganda for Gorbachev's anti-alcohol drive.
evt-su-perestroika-policy: A 1988 Soviet stamp emblazoned "ПЕРЕСТРОЙКА" (Perestroika) with a determined worker and scenes of industry, the reform sold as a renewal of socialism.
evt-su-glasnost-policy: Crowds press around the "Wall of Sorrow," papered with photos and names of Stalin's Gulag victims, at the first Soviet exhibition on the crimes of Stalinism, glasnost made visible.
evt-su-chernobyl: Chernobyl's wrecked Reactor 4, encased in the hastily built concrete-and-steel "sarcophagus" that still sealed in the ruined core years after the 1986 explosion.
evt-su-revolutions-1989: An armed civilian on the street during Romania's December 1989 revolution, the one violent overthrow in a year of otherwise peaceful collapse across the Eastern Bloc.
evt-su-solidarity-poland: Lech Wałęsa addresses the August 1980 strike inside the Gdańsk shipyard, beneath the Polish eagle and a poster of the workers' "21 demands" ("21 x TAK"), the birth of Solidarity.
evt-su-berlin-wall-falls: Crowds stand atop the Berlin Wall at the Brandenburg Gate in November 1989, the barrier turned overnight into a stage for its own demolition.
evt-su-german-reunification: "DANKE GORBI! 3.10.90" painted on a wall by a tank turret, German thanks to Gorbachev on reunification day, 3 October 1990.
evt-su-baltic-way: Estonians, Latvians and Lithuanians link hands in the Baltic Way human chain, 23 August 1989, holding a national tricolor and a black mourning flag.
evt-su-nagorno-karabakh: An Azerbaijani refugee family shelters in a train carriage, displaced by the Armenian-Azerbaijani war over Nagorno-Karabakh, the first ethnic war to tear at the Soviet Union.
evt-su-congress-peoples-deputies: Boris Yeltsin works a crowd in early 1989; the blunt populist won his Moscow seat in the Congress elections with roughly 90 percent of the vote.
evt-su-sakharov-recall: Andrei Sakharov and his wife Elena Bonner arriving in the West in June 1989, free to travel after Gorbachev ended his internal exile.
evt-su-article-6-repealed: The Congress of People's Deputies in 1989, the elected body of the perestroika era that soon voted to end the Communist Party's constitutional monopoly on power.
evt-su-gorbachev-president: Mikhail Gorbachev, the reformer who made himself the first and only President of the USSR, an office that proved too weak to save the Union.
evt-su-novo-ogarevo: The ballot for the March 1991 all-Union referendum, asking voters whether to preserve the USSR as a 'renewed federation' — the mandate Gorbachev took into the Novo-Ogaryovo talks.
evt-su-august-coup: Crowds and improvised barricades ring the Russian 'White House' parliament during the August 1991 coup, the rallying point Yeltsin made the center of resistance.
evt-su-yeltsin-russian-president: Boris Yeltsin's official portrait as President of Russia, the office a popular vote handed him in June 1991.
evt-su-party-banned: A Communist Party of the Soviet Union membership card from 1989, Lenin's profile inside the cover — the badge of the organization Yeltsin banned and Gorbachev quit leading in 1991.
evt-su-ukraine-referendum: The actual ballot for Ukraine's 1 December 1991 independence referendum, asking voters to confirm the Act of Independence.
evt-su-belovezha: The leaders of Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus sign the Belovezha Accords on 8 December 1991, dissolving the USSR at a Belarusian hunting lodge.
evt-su-alma-ata-protocol: Republic leaders at Alma-Ata in December 1991 — Yeltsin, Kravchuk, Nazarbayev, Shushkevich among them — where the protocol that created the Commonwealth of Independent States was signed.
evt-su-gorbachev-resigns: Mikhail Gorbachev addresses an audience from the podium — the Soviet leader who resigned the presidency on 25 December 1991.
evt-su-soviet-flag-down: The Kremlin Senate dome and its flagpole — where the Soviet flag was lowered for the last time on 25 December 1991 and the Russian tricolor (flying here) raised in its place.
evt-su-dissolution: Boris Yeltsin waves the Russian tricolor at the White House on 22 August 1991 — the defining image of the end of Soviet power and the rise of the state that outlived the USSR.
evt-ac-peiligang-culture: A reconstructed red pottery jar made by the Peiligang culture, unearthed near Xinzheng in Henan province.
evt-ac-millet-cultivation: Harvested foxtail millet — the small golden grain that was northern China's staple crop for thousands of years.
evt-ac-cishan-culture: Stone tools of the Cishan culture on museum display — polished implements and grinding stones used for daily work and processing grain.
evt-ac-rice-domestication: Charred rice grains from a Chinese Neolithic site, preserved by burning and displayed under a museum magnifier.
evt-ac-bone-flutes: A Neolithic crane-bone flute from Jiahu in Wuyang, Henan — the oldest playable musical instrument ever found, its finger holes still visible.
evt-ac-jiahu-symbols: An inscribed tortoise shell from Jiahu — the kind of carved-symbol object at the center of the proto-writing debate.
evt-ac-yangshao-pottery: A close-up of the famous Yangshao "human face and fish" motif painted on a Banpo basin — a round face flanked by stylized fish, one of the iconic images of Chinese prehistory.
evt-ac-banpo-village: A museum diorama reconstructing the Banpo settlement, showing the cluster of round thatched pit houses around a larger central building.
evt-ac-banpo-symbols: A chart of the incised geometric marks found on Yangshao pottery rims at Banpo — strokes, crosses, and hooks that look systematic but have never been read as writing.
evt-ac-hemudu-culture: A Hemudu-culture black pottery cauldron, a characteristic vessel from the Yangtze delta wetland villages.
evt-ac-silk-origins: A cocoon of the domesticated silkworm Bombyx mori — the single continuous filament wound here is what Neolithic Chinese learned to unwind into silk thread.
evt-ac-fuxi: A silk painting of Fuxi and his sister-wife Nüwa, their serpent tails intertwined — the half-human, half-serpent pair, holding the set-square and compasses of earth and heaven.
evt-ac-shennong: A traditional woodcut of Shennong, the Divine Farmer, dressed in leaves and tasting a sprig of a plant — the mythic image of the ruler who sampled herbs to test them.
evt-ac-hongshan-jade: The dark-green Hongshan "C-dragon," carved from nephrite jade and unearthed in Inner Mongolia in 1971 — the headline object of Neolithic Chinese jade-working.
evt-ac-pig-dragon: A Hongshan jade pig-dragon (zhulong): coiled body, blunt pig snout, a slit eye, and a central hole for suspension — the earliest known dragon image in Chinese art.
evt-ac-ancestor-worship-origins: A reconstructed Hongshan painted pottery vessel from Liaoning — the kind of food-and-drink container placed in graves to provision the dead, an early signature of ancestor worship.
evt-ac-liangzhu: The "Cong King" — the largest jade cong ever found at Liangzhu, from the richest tomb at Fanshan. Its squared, ringed body is the signature object of the culture.
evt-ac-jade-bi-cong: A Liangzhu jade bi — a flat, mottled-green disc with a central bore, the form later tradition tied to heaven.
evt-ac-liangzhu-symbols: A Liangzhu pottery jar bearing incised symbols, displayed at the Liangzhu Museum with the marks drawn out above it.
evt-ac-longshan-pottery: A Longshan eggshell-thin black stem cup — walls under a millimeter, made for ritual rather than use.
evt-ac-walled-towns: The stone east gate and citadel wall at Shimao (c. 2300–2100 BCE), the largest fortified Longshan-era town.
evt-ac-yellow-emperor: A traditional Chinese portrait of the Yellow Emperor — a legendary figure with no real likeness, shown as later artists imagined him.
evt-ac-battle-zhuolu: A traditional depiction of Chi You, the horned, beast-like warrior the Yellow Emperor defeats at Zhuolu.
evt-ac-cangjie: A traditional portrait of Cangjie, legendary inventor of Chinese writing — a mythic figure shown as later painters imagined him.
evt-ac-scapulimancy: An early Chinese divination bone — a heated, cracked scapula of the kind read for messages from the ancestors.
evt-ac-jade-trade-networks: A notched jade disk of the Longshan culture (2400–1900 BCE) — the kind of prestige object that moved across Neolithic China.
evt-ac-taosi-observatory: Excavation of the rammed-earth observatory platform at Taosi in Shanxi — its arc of pillar foundations used to track the sun.
evt-ac-great-flood: The Yellow River in violent, silt-choked flood at Hukou Falls — the river whose floods Chinese tradition remembers as the disaster that launched the first dynasty.
evt-ac-yu-the-great: A traditional later portrait of Yu the Great on silk — there is no contemporary likeness of the semi-legendary figure, only depictions handed down by much later tradition.
evt-ac-xia-founding: A Xia-period pottery jue, a three-legged ritual wine vessel — the kind of everyday-yet-ceremonial object that survives from the era tradition assigns to China's first dynasty.
evt-ac-xia-calendar: A printed traditional Chinese lunisolar calendar from the Qing era — a tangible descendant of the month-and-season system tradition traces back to the Xia.
evt-ac-erlitou-palace: A bronze jue (tripod wine cup) excavated at Erlitou in 1984 — the kind of ritual object cast in the workshops of China's earliest palace town.
evt-ac-xia-bronze: A late-Xia bronze ding (tripod cauldron), an early Chinese ritual vessel cast by the piece-mold method that began at Erlitou.
evt-ac-turquoise-mosaic: The Erlitou turquoise dragon as excavated — over 2,000 turquoise chips, about 27 inches (70 cm) long, found resting on the body of an elite man.
evt-ac-xia-roads: A turquoise-inlaid bronze plaque excavated at Erlitou (grave 81YLVM4) — turquoise hauled in from over 620 miles (1,000 km) away, worked into an animal-mask design.
evt-ac-jie-of-xia: An 18th-century painted album leaf illustrating Jie's legendary "pool of wine, forest of meat" — the lurid scene that made him China's archetypal fallen tyrant.
evt-ac-battle-mingtiao: A later hanging-scroll portrait of King Tang of Shang, the founder whose victory at Mingtiao began the Shang dynasty.
evt-susa-founded: Painted pottery from the earliest Susa (around 4000 BCE) — a beaker and dish with the geometric designs that made the city's craft famous. Louvre.
evt-proto-elamite-script: A Proto-Elamite (Susa III) account tablet — round number-impressions and still-undeciphered signs (Louvre).
evt-anshan-city: A Proto-Elamite silver figure of a kneeling bull holding a spouted vessel (around 3000 BCE) — a masterpiece of the highland Iranian world Anshan dominated. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
